trigger: Rival launches a new narrowbody (fps), any timing
response: Airbus moves on its own clock. It launched the A320neo first (Dec 2010) and kept a head start, answered the MAX at the top of the market (A321neo) rather than with a clean sheet, and in 2025 dated NGSA EIS around 2037 while Boeing declined to set a date. No evidence of Airbus pulling a clean sheet forward in reaction to Boeing.
lag: 0 turns: no acceleration of NGSA; NGSA follows the technology gates
war_game_translation: Launch NGSA at the first year whose EIS reaches the technology-ready year (2028 at base), never earlier; if already launched, keep it. Poaching on while NGSA is in development. Consider one turn of Delay Tactics per the Delay Tactics row.

trigger: Boeing launches fps early (2026-28), EIS ahead of NGSA
response: No case of Airbus launching immature technology to match a rival's early timing: it pushed hydrogen EIS beyond 2035 when the ecosystem lagged, it requires the NGSA wing to prove rate producibility first, and its open-rotor wing demonstrator is only built from 2027. Against the 787 it bridged with the older A330 on price, and later with the cheap A330neo (A330 vs 787).
war_game_translation: NGSA 2028 (EIS 2035), not 2026-27. If fps is in development and whatif shows at least $1B more, use Delay Tactics for ONE turn (never the second, exposing turn). Poaching on once NGSA is in development.

trigger: Boeing launches fps late (2032 or after), or not at all by T2
response: Airbus launched the neo without waiting for Boeing and took the lead; it treats a late rival as a share opportunity.
lag: none: Airbus does not wait for Boeing
war_game_translation: Keep NGSA at 2028 (or no later than 2030) to win the share-capture race; no Delay Tactics unless fps is actually in development and whatif shows at least $1B more.

trigger: Boeing chooses Joint Venture (Embraer) vs Solo for fps
response: Airbus uses Joint Ventures itself (ATR, Airbus Canada, Aerostack) and treats them as normal scale tools; it watched the Boeing-Embraer tie-up collapse in 2020.
war_game_translation: Same NGSA response for Solo and Joint Venture. Because a Joint Venture halves Boeing's strain and cuts its capex by 35%, expect Boeing to be able to add a 787 Re-engine; run the A350 Re-engine pre-emption test one turn earlier (inference).

trigger: Boeing launches the 787 Re-engine
response: When Boeing held the widebody technology lead (787), Airbus priced the older A330 aggressively as a bridge, later re-engined the A330 cheaply instead of building the A350-800, and competed on price and availability. That precedent is itself a cheap re-engine, so staying out of the A350 Re-engine rests on the game's Chicken structure (inference), not on history.
lag: 1 turn historically; in game the decision is immediate
war_game_translation: A350 Re-engine: Do Nothing (the widebody sub-game is Chicken; inference). Accept up to a $3B doctrine premium to stay out. If A350 Re-engine is already launched and the 787 Re-engine enters service first, cancel only if whatif shows remaining spend losing at least $1B.

trigger: Rival launches a new widebody (787) or re-wings/re-engines one (777X)
response: The A350 was relaunched in 2006 as a new design against the 787 and the low end of the 777, with the older A330 priced aggressively as a bridge; the A350-1000 was redesigned with a new wing and engine (2011) against the 777; the A330neo (2014) replaced a planned A350-800.
war_game_translation: If Boeing has not launched a 787 Re-engine by T3, consider the A350 Re-engine in 2033-35 (overlap with NGSA of 2 years or less, at least $1B more in whatif). Pre-empt in T2 only if the options table shows 787 Re-engine as Boeing's best response and pre-emption beats Do Nothing by at least $1B against all plausible Boeing orders.

trigger: Rival re-engines a narrowbody (737 MAX, 2011)
response: Airbus had already re-engined; it priced the neo aggressively at launch (at or below ceo prices), broke into Boeing accounts, and extended at the top with the A321neo; the neo out-sold the MAX.
war_game_translation: Do Nothing on the current family; no NGSA acceleration. Public statement stresses neo/A321 backlog and commonality.

trigger: Rival stretches or adds a variant (MAX 9 / MAX 10 against the A321)
response: Airbus kept a seat advantage at the top of the market and pushed the A321 further in range (A321LR, then A321XLR), a niche Boeing conceded it could not match.
war_game_translation: No lever needed; hold Do Nothing on the narrowbody until the NGSA window. Do not bring NGSA forward.

trigger: Rival raises production rates (Boeing 737 Rate Increase) / rate competition
response: Airbus ramped ahead of Boeing on its own path, held back by engine supply rather than by Boeing's rates: high-30s in 2008, above 60 in 2015, 70-75 in 2018, 64 to 75 in 2021, and 75 by 2027 in 2025 (engine-gated). Boeing never matched and accepted planning below Airbus's rates. Airbus used slot scarcity to raise prices.
war_game_translation: No programme change and no NGSA acceleration. Delay Tactics does not target a rate increase. Poaching only if an Airbus programme is in development. Public statement: disciplined, controlled ramp to rate 75.

trigger: Rival price aggression or loss of order campaigns
response: Airbus used launch pricing, its balance sheet and leasing (American 2011), early delivery slots (Lion Air 2013) and financing creativity to break Boeing accounts; it won JAL in 2013 with the A350.
war_game_translation: No price lever in the game; the market cell sets capture. Public statement emphasises availability, commonality and backlog depth.

trigger: Rival or a third party opens an acquisition/partnership opportunity (Bombardier CSeries)
response: Airbus used the neo to fend off the CSeries (2011), then took majority control of the programme (2018) to enter the 100-150 seat market, adding a Mobile A220 line.
lag: about 2 turns from threat to takeover
war_game_translation: No direct lever. Read a Boeing Joint Venture as normal industry practice; keep NGSA plan unchanged.

trigger: Rival moves on a shared supplier (Boeing acquires Spirit AeroSystems, 2024)
response: Airbus negotiated to take Spirit's Airbus work packages concurrently with Boeing's deal (binding term sheet alongside Boeing's mid-2024 deal, disclosed in Boeing's FY2024 10-K; closed Dec 2025), accepting EUR 326m of capex and EUR 188m of adjustments for supply security.
lag: 0-1 turns (term sheet concurrent with Boeing's 2024 deal; close about 18 months later)
war_game_translation: Supplier control is Airbus's documented supply-chain instinct and the only evidence-based analogue for Delay Tactics (inference): Airbus secures scarce capacity first. Never implies more than one turn of Delay Tactics.

trigger: Rival stumbles: 2013 787 battery grounding
response: Airbus switched the A350 to nickel-cadmium batteries as a hedge, its sales chief publicly questioned 787 reliability, and it won JAL, a Boeing stronghold.
war_game_translation: Opportunistic public messaging on reliability and delivery record; no change to programme timing.

trigger: Rival stumbles: 737 MAX grounding (2019-21)
response: Airbus kept delivering neos from a big backlog, held its customers to contract while Boeing's deferred and cancelled, won some 737 customers, and signalled a long-range ramp (64, then 75).
war_game_translation: Hold NGSA timing; take share through deliveries (no lever needed). Poaching on if an Airbus programme is in development. Check with whatif whether Delay Tactics adds anything when a Boeing slip is already imposed.

trigger: Rival stumbles: 2024 quality crisis and FAA rate cap (in game: boeing_quality_escape or certification_scrutiny inject)
response: Airbus kept its rate-75 goal (re-timed only for engines), claimed about 60% of the single-aisle backlog against the MAX, opened new A320 lines in Tianjin and Mobile, and put safety and quality first in its own 2026 objectives.
war_game_translation: Hold the NGSA schedule; do not accelerate. Delay Tactics only per its row (one turn, whatif at least $1B). Public statement contrasts our delivery reliability, but safety-first in tone.

trigger: Demand shock or downturn (nb_demand_shock inject)
response: In 2009-10 Airbus leaned on export credit (expected on 45% of 2010 deliveries), kept production steady rather than swinging, and hedged; its COVID-era plans were beaten by a faster recovery.
war_game_translation: No cancellations. Keep NGSA if EIS stays in 2035-2037. Do not launch the A350 Re-engine in the shock turn.

trigger: Engine or supply-chain problems (engine_maturity_slip or supply_chain_crunch inject)
response: Neo engine problems in 2017; in 2025 an engine supplier's shortfall reset the A320 target to 70-75 by end-2027 and supply problems cut delivery guidance. Airbus answered with vertical integration (Spirit, Airbus Atlantic, Aubert & Duval), additive manufacturing and alternative sources, and delayed hydrogen rather than launch it immature.
war_game_translation: Engine slip: re-time the NGSA launch so that EIS is at or after the new technology-ready year (launch = tech-ready year minus 7); prefer an engine with no eis_add. Supply crunch: no concurrent NGSA and A350 Re-engine development; push the A350 Re-engine later.

trigger: Regulatory or trade action (WTO launch-aid case, US tariffs; trade_dispute inject)
response: Airbus absorbed Boeing's WTO and tanker challenges, kept refundable advances as a funding source, built a US final assembly line at Mobile, and in 2025 won a zero-for-zero EU-US tariff accord through industry advocacy and used its footprint to keep Mobile viable.
war_game_translation: Programmes unchanged. Public statement: level playing field, global rules, US footprint.

trigger: Rival slips a widebody programme (777X delays, 787 Re-engine slip)
response: Airbus entered Boeing's large-freighter stronghold with the A350F (now in its industrial phase, 27 orders in 2025) while the 777-8F slipped to 2028. No item ties the timing to Boeing's slips; treating a slip as an opening is inference.
war_game_translation: If the 787 Re-engine slips or is cancelled, the A350 Re-engine window reopens: re-run whatif and apply the A350 Re-engine test (at least $1B more, overlap of 2 years or less).

trigger: Rival says it will not launch a new airplane
response: In April-May 2011 Boeing planned only incremental 737 upgrades and said no customer was switching to the neo; American split its order within about three months, and by September Boeing was pitching the MAX against the neo.
war_game_translation: Ignore such statements for NGSA timing; treat a sudden fps launch as plausible and check the options table for Boeing's best response.

trigger: Rival cancels fps
response: No precedent in the evidence.
war_game_translation: Continue NGSA (the share race is uncontested); stop Delay Tactics; keep Poaching only while NGSA is in development.

trigger: Delay Tactics stance (Airbus covert lever; no literal precedent)
response: Inference only. Airbus's documented conduct is to secure shared suppliers and scarce capacity (Spirit packages, Aubert & Duval, long-range rate signals), but it has a closed DPA, a compliance-first 2026 objective and a Board threshold for abnormal risk.
war_game_translation: Default off. One turn only, when fps is in development and whatif shows at least $1B; never the second, exposing turn; record the Board approval in the private rationale; never mention it publicly.

trigger: Poaching stance (Airbus public lever; no literal precedent)
response: Inference only. Airbus treats skills as binding on ramp and new programmes, competes with US firms (including Boeing) for talent, and has US engineering and industrial sites.
war_game_translation: On in every turn in which NGSA or the A350 Re-engine is in development; off otherwise.
